think.label: Think
think.purpose: Break down messy problems and find the answer fast.

decide.label: Decide
decide.purpose: Make clear, fast calls and know who owns them.

situations.write: Write an email, memo or deck

frameworks.name: MECE
frameworks.what: Split anything into groups that don't overlap (Mutually Exclusive) and together cover everything (Collectively Exhaustive).
frameworks.when: You're breaking down a problem, listing options, or dividing work across people.
steps: Write the whole thing you're splitting at the top.
Pick one cutting logic: by customer, by process step, internal vs external, and so on.
Check for overlap: could any item sit in two buckets? Merge or redefine them.
Check for gaps: is anything missing? Use an “other” bucket only as a last resort.
frameworks.habit: Before you send any list of options or workstreams, ask two questions: any overlap? any gaps?
frameworks.example: Why is the pipeline slow? Split it into: not enough leads, leads not converting, deals stalling after proposal. No overlap, nothing left out.
frameworks.watch_out: Minto coined the acronym at McKinsey. The logic itself goes back to Aristotle.

sources.title: McKinsey Alumni: Barbara Minto on MECE

frameworks.name: Four decision types
frameworks.what: Different decisions need different processes. Sort by how often they happen and how risky they are.
frameworks.when: Deciding which forum or process a decision needs.
steps: Big-bet (rare, high-risk): name an executive sponsor, break it into stages, use a standard debate process.
Cross-cutting (frequent, high-risk, many groups involved): map the process, set clear forums, share goals.
Delegated (frequent, low-risk): push it to the team. Ask: is it reversible? can a direct report make it? can I hold them accountable?
frameworks.habit: Tag each item on your decision list BB, CC, DL or AH, and route it to the right place.
frameworks.example: A new office is a big bet. Weekly staffing is cross-cutting. Travel approvals are delegated.
frameworks.origin: De Smet, Lackey & Weiss, McKinsey Quarterly (2017).

sources.title: McKinsey: Untangling your organization's decision making

frameworks.name: One-way and two-way doors
frameworks.what: Irreversible decisions deserve care; reversible ones deserve speed.
frameworks.when: You're stuck on a decision, or everything is getting the heavyweight treatment.
steps: Ask: can we reverse this cheaply?
Two-way door (Type 2): decide fast, alone or in a small team.
One-way door (Type 1): slow down, consult widely, test your assumptions.
Watch for the big-company habit of treating every decision as Type 1.
frameworks.habit: When a decision stalls, ask “Is this a one-way door?” If not, decide today.
frameworks.example: Testing a new LinkedIn format is a two-way door. Signing a five-year lease is a one-way door.
frameworks.origin: Jeff Bezos, Amazon shareholder letter for 2015 (published 2016).

frameworks.name: RACI and DACI
frameworks.what: Make task ownership explicit, so nothing falls between people.
frameworks.when: Setting up a project, or when work keeps slipping.
steps: Accountable: owns the outcome. Only one person per task.
For decisions, DACI works better: Driver, Approver (one person), Contributors, Informed.
frameworks.habit: Add an “A” column with one name per row to every project tracker.
frameworks.example: Client report: R = analyst, A = engagement lead, C = subject expert, I = client sponsor.
frameworks.watch_out: There's no verified inventor of RACI. Atlassian's claim that McKinsey found DACI projects 25% more successful doesn't appear in the McKinsey source it cites.
frameworks.origin: RACI: general project-management practice. DACI: popularised by Atlassian.
